voiceover.text: Last time, the protective factors for sleep turned out to be mostly conditions. Today, the personal skills that protect health, and what they need to work. First, think of one health change you made and kept, and one you tried and didn't keep. Write one sentence on what was different. Not what you did, but the situation, the support, or what you believed at the time.

The first skill is self-efficacy: your belief that you can do the specific thing a goal needs. It's about capability, not worth, so don't confuse it with self-esteem. And it's task-specific. You might be sure you can keep a lights-out time on school nights, and unsure you can ask a doctor a question. It predicts three things: whether you attempt a change at all, how hard you try, and most importantly, whether you start again after a slip. Two people can lapse the same way, and the one who believes the goal is reachable starts again.

scenes.title: four sources, and the runner who quit

voiceover.text: Self-efficacy is built from four sources, and they're not equal. Mastery experience, having succeeded at something similar, is by far the strongest. Seeing someone like you succeed helps, but the likeness matters, so watching an elite athlete does less for a beginner. Being told you can do it, by someone credible, is weaker, and it collapses if experience says otherwise. And how you read your body counts: a racing heart can mean readiness, not inability. Take a student who started running three times, quit three times, and now says, I'm just not a runner. What's missing is mastery. So design the first week to be achievable.

The second skill is health literacy, and it's much wider than reading a leaflet. It's four abilities: find, understand, evaluate and use health information and services. Find means knowing a service exists, and that you're allowed to use it. Understand means making sense of a dose or a risk. Evaluate is the critical step: is the source reliable, and who benefits if you believe it? A sleep supplement promising fast results, with a discount code, fails that straight away. Use means acting on it, including asking again when something wasn't clear. And it's shared. A clinician who explains clearly raises the health literacy of every patient they see.

The third skill is help-seeking, reaching out for support, formal or informal. Almost every issue we've met gets worse with delay and better with early contact, yet many young people delay seeking help, or never seek it. Five common barriers stand in the way: stigma, not recognising the problem, not knowing where to go, fear of what happens next, like judgement or parents being told, and preferring to handle it alone. Three things reliably help: one trusted adult, knowing exactly where to go, and having done it before with a good result, which is mastery again.

scenes.title: protecting others, and the limit of the skill

voiceover.text: The syllabus says themselves and others. A young person who can say, I think this is bigger than me, let's go together, has protected two people, as long as they know the limit of what a friend can carry. But here's the limit of the skill itself. Telling someone to seek help where there's a six-month wait and nothing after hours teaches them that seeking help doesn't work, and that lesson lasts. The skill and the service have to be built together.

The fourth skill is problem-solving. Most health decisions young people make aren't really decided, they're defaulted, in the moment, under pressure. Problem-solving gives you a structure in advance. Define the real problem: I'm always exhausted could be sleep, workload or mood, and each has a different fix. Generate several options. Weigh what each costs, risks and protects, including friendships. Choose and act. Then review, the step everyone skips. The most useful version is a pre-decided response, like a sentence ready for your manager: I can't work past nine on school nights. Rehearsed words are there under pressure, and good intentions often aren't.

scenes.title: what the skills can and cannot do

voiceover.text: So what can these skills do? Within the same circumstances, they change outcomes. Two young people in identical conditions, one who knows where to go, believes it'll help, and has the words ready, won't end up with the same health. But skills can't create a service, pay for one, provide a trusted adult, or make a street safe. So a program that teaches only skills is taken up most easily by those who already have the conditions, and it can lift the average and widen the gap. The fix is pairing: teach help-seeking and fund the service, teach critical health literacy and regulate the marketing. Look at your kept change: was the difference a skill, or a condition?
Two things to remember. Four skills, four jobs: try and restart, find and judge, early not late, decided not defaulted. And skills work inside conditions, they don't create them.

Two exam questions. First. A student knows a friend is drinking heavily most weekends, and doesn't know whether to say something, or to whom. Identify the skill or skills that would most help, explain how it would change the outcome, and name the condition it needs to work. Pause here to answer.

Problem-solving, joined with help-seeking for someone else; either earns the mark if you explain how. It turns say nothing or confront into real options: talk to the friend, go with them to an adult, or ask for advice without naming them. The condition is a service that advises about someone else's drinking, and a school where raising it isn't dobbing. The classic mistake is naming the skill and stopping there.
Second. Teaching young people health skills is the most effective way to improve their health. Assess this statement. Pause here to answer.

Judge the word most. Credit the case first: the skills change outcomes, can be taught, and last into adulthood. Then the problem: each skill works inside conditions it doesn't create, so a skills-only program lifts the average and can widen the gap. Judge it necessary, but not sufficient, and best paired with conditions. The classic mistake is agreeing or disagreeing with the whole statement.
So, for any skill, say what it changes, how it protects you and someone else, and the condition it needs. Next, five more skills, starting with the one adults recommend most: resilience.
